title: Bird flu reaches Australia, completing global spread - Farm Progress
snippet: Farm Progress America: The H5N1 avian influenza virus has now been detected on every continent, with Australia confirming its first cases in wild seabirds last week. Australia's status as the last continent free from the current H5N1 strain ended when officials confirmed the virus in two wild seabirds near Esperance, Western Australia. Australian Egg Minister Julie Collins emphasized that there is "no evidence the virus has reached the country's poultry or ag systems," and no trade restrictions have been imposed on Australian poultry exports. Australian farmers remember last year's H7 outbreak that forced the culling of 1.8 million birds and created egg shortages lasting nearly a year. Western Australian poultry groups have already canceled summer bird shows and urged producers to restrict bird movements and keep flocks separated from wild birds. The virus has killed millions of wild birds worldwide and infected commercial poultry, dairy operations, and some farm workers.

Avian flu — which, in another, milder strain is much like the common cold in wild birds — morphed and became pathogenic when chickens and other poultry at industrial-scale producers were exposed to the virus through contact with migrating flocks of wild birds. Since it first appeared in Europe in 2020, this “Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza” strain has devastated wildlife worldwide, the largest avian flu outbreak ever. And this panzootic is obviously not over. [...] Some of the wildlife victims are endangered species, and this virus’s ability to spread to new hosts is astounding. As of December 2025, H5N1 had infected some 598 types of bird and 102 mammal species, according to the United Nations. The numbers have jumped substantially over the past 18 months: As of August 2024, the U.N. tally was 485 bird and 48 mammal species.

title: Birds in Frozen Waters: Should We Help Them or Not When They Look Trapped? - Indian Defence Review
snippet: The decision to intervene or walk away now carries implications that extend from local ponds to international poultry markets and the evolving trajectory of a virus that has fundamentally changed how wild birds live and die. **Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1**, first detected as a global threat nearly three decades ago, is no longer an episodic visitor to wild bird populations. Based on surveillance data from multiple states and European veterinary authorities, the virus is now considered **endemic in waterfowl**, circulating continuously through migration flyways and wintering grounds. As reported on MDR , among numerous wild birds found dead this winter, officials confirmed avian influenza in a significant proportion, with swans disproportionately represented. The finding aligns with broader surveillance: waterfowl serve as natural reservoirs, shedding virus while migrating, and congregating on remaining open water creates ideal **transmission conditions**. Wild bird mortality is systematically undercounted, but surveillance programs confirm elevated carcass numbers, particularly among swans and raptors.

title: Agriculture officials urge hiked biosecurity to protect birds from avian influenza - Big Island Now
snippet: A recent presumptive case of avian influenza in a duck on O‘ahu prompts a reminder from Hawai‘i Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity Animal Industry Division urging commercial poultry operations and backyard bird owners to increase biosecurity measures to protect their flocks from avian influenza — or highly pathogenic avian influenza. Backyard poultry, ducks and other birds can get avian influenza if they have contact with infected wild birds or share food, sources of water and environments with them. To report multiple or unusual illnesses in poultry, livestock or other wild birds or animals, contact Hawai‘i Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity Animal Industry Division at 808-483-7100 from 7 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday to Friday or via email at **dabic@hawaii.gov**.
